body.ja:
「敦盛」は、源平の一ノ谷の戦い (1184年) の一場面を語る幸若舞の曲である。源氏の武将熊谷直実は、海へ逃れようとする平家の若武者を呼び止め、組み伏せて首を取ろうとした。兜を上げると、我が子と同じ十六、七の美しい若者——平敦盛であった。

直実は逃がそうとしたが、味方の軍勢が迫っていた。「どうせ他の者の手にかかるなら」と泣く泣く首を取った。敦盛の腰には笛があり、夜明け前に平家の陣から聞こえていた笛の音はこの若者のものだったと知る。直実は世の無常を悟り、のちに出家した。

曲の中で直実は「人間五十年、下天のうちをくらぶれば、夢幻のごとくなり」と嘆く。人の世の五十年など、天上の時の流れに比べれば夢か幻のようなものだ——[[p:織田信長]]はこの一節を好み、桶狭間に出陣する朝に舞ったと『信長公記』は伝える。信長は四十九歳で本能寺に死んだ。
body.en:
Atsumori is a kōwaka ballad telling a scene from the battle of Ichinotani (1184) in the war of the Minamoto and Taira. The Minamoto warrior Kumagai Naozane called back a young Taira knight fleeing to the ships, threw him down and raised his helmet to take his head — and found a beautiful youth of sixteen or so, his own son's age: Taira no Atsumori.

Naozane wanted to let him go, but his own side's horsemen were coming. "If he must die at another's hand," he wept, and took the head. At the boy's waist was a flute; the music heard from the Taira camp before dawn had been his. Naozane, seeing how fleeting the world is, later became a monk.

In the ballad he laments: "Fifty years of a man's life, beside the realm below heaven, are a dream, an illusion." [[p:織田信長|Oda Nobunaga]] loved these lines and danced them on the morning he rode out to Okehazama, says his chronicle. He died at Honnōji at forty-nine.

title.en: Linked verse, and the hundred verses of Atago

body.ja:
連歌は、何人もが集まって五七五の句と七七の句を交互に詠みつないでいく歌である。武将や商人、公家が身分をこえて同じ座に連なり、教養と機知を競った。茶の湯と並ぶ、戦国の社交の場であった。

1582年五月、[[p:明智光秀]]は京の愛宕山で連歌の会を開いた。その発句は「時は今 あめが下しる 五月かな」。「時 (とき)」は光秀の家である土岐氏に、「あめが下しる」は「天が下 (天下) を治める」に通じる——後の人々は、本能寺の変を前にした光秀の決意が込められていたと読んだ。

その十日ほど後、光秀は本能寺の信長を襲った。もっとも、この読み方は後から付けられたもので、本当に光秀がそう考えていたかは分からない。
body.en:
Renga, linked verse, was composed by a gathering, each poet capping the last with a verse of 5-7-5 or 7-7 syllables. Warriors, merchants and court nobles sat together beyond their ranks to match learning and wit — with tea, the great social art of the age of war.

In the fifth month of 1582 [[p:明智光秀|Akechi Mitsuhide]] held a renga gathering on Mount Atago near Kyoto. His opening verse ran: "Now is the time / to rule all under the rain / in the fifth month." "Time" (toki) sounds like Toki, the house of Mitsuhide's forebears; "all under the rain" (ame ga shita) sounds like "all under heaven". Later readers took it as his resolve before Honnōji.

Ten days or so later he attacked Nobunaga at Honnōji. The reading, though, was put on the verse afterwards; whether Mitsuhide meant it so, no one knows.

body.ja:
1576年、[[p:織田信長]]は琵琶湖の東岸、安土山に城を築き始め、三年後に移り住んだ。京にも美濃にも近く、湖の舟で物を運べる要の地である。

城の中心には、五層七重の「天主」がそびえた。外から見れば五重、中は地下を含めて七階。最上階は金色の四角い部屋、その下は朱塗りの八角形の部屋で、壁と襖には[[p:狩野永徳]]の一門が描いた絵が並んだ。宣教師フロイスは「ヨーロッパにもこれほどの建物はない」と書き残している。高い石垣の上に天守を載せる城の形は、ここから全国に広がった。

城下には楽市楽座の掟が出され、商人が集まった。だが1582年、本能寺の変の直後、天主は原因の分からない火事で焼け落ちた。安土城は完成からわずか三年で姿を消した。
body.en:
In 1576 [[p:織田信長|Oda Nobunaga]] began a castle on Mount Azuchi on the east shore of Lake Biwa and moved in three years later — a key site near both Kyoto and Mino, with the lake for shipping.

At its heart rose a seven-storey "tenshu": five roofs outside, seven floors within, counting the basement. The top floor was a golden square room, the one below a vermilion octagon, and the walls and screens were covered with paintings by [[p:狩野永徳|Kanō Eitoku]]'s school. The missionary Frois wrote that Europe had no building to match it. The castle with a tall keep on high stone walls spread from here across the country.

Below it the town had its free-market laws and filled with merchants. But in 1582, just after Honnōji, the keep burned down from causes no one knows. Azuchi had stood only three years.

body.ja:
1583年、豊臣秀吉は石山本願寺の跡地に大坂城を築き始めた。数万の人夫を使い、各地の大名に石を運ばせた。黒漆に金箔の瓦と金の飾りで飾った天守は、天下人の力を示すものであった。

城は外側を堀と曲輪で幾重にも囲まれ、難攻不落と言われた。1614年の冬の陣でも徳川の大軍は攻めあぐね、[[p:真田信繁]]が城の南に築いた出丸 (真田丸) は敵を寄せつけなかった。

しかし和議の条件として外堀を、さらに内堀まで埋められると、大坂城は裸の城となった。1615年の夏の陣で城は燃え落ち、豊臣家は滅んだ。徳川家はのちに、豊臣の城の上に土を盛って埋め、その上に新しい大坂城を築いた。
body.en:
In 1583 Toyotomi Hideyoshi began Osaka castle on the site of the Ishiyama Honganji, with tens of thousands of labourers and stone hauled by lords from every province. Its keep, black lacquer with gold-leafed tiles and golden ornaments, proclaimed the power of the ruler of the realm.

Ringed with moats and baileys, it was called impregnable. In the winter campaign of 1614 the great Tokugawa army could make no headway, and the outwork [[p:真田信繁|Sanada Nobushige]] built south of the castle — the Sanada-maru — kept the enemy at bay.

But as the price of peace the outer moat, and then the inner, were filled in, and Osaka stood naked. In the summer campaign of 1615 it burned and the Toyotomi were gone. The Tokugawa later buried the Toyotomi castle under earth and built a new Osaka castle on top of it.

body.ja:
1586年、関白となった豊臣秀吉は京の内野に、城と御殿を兼ねた壮麗な邸宅「聚楽第」を築き始め、翌年完成させた。「長生不老の楽しみを聚める」という意味の名である。

1588年には後陽成天皇を聚楽第に迎え、諸大名に天皇の前で秀吉への忠誠を誓わせた。天皇の行幸を受けることは、秀吉が天下人であることを世に示す大きな儀式であった。

その後、秀吉は聚楽第を甥で後継ぎの関白豊臣秀次に譲った。ところが1595年、秀吉に実子秀頼が生まれていたこともあって秀次は謀反の疑いをかけられて切腹させられ、聚楽第は跡形もなく取り壊された。わずか八年の栄華であった。
body.en:
In 1586, newly regent, Toyotomi Hideyoshi began a splendid palace-fortress in Kyoto, the Jurakudai — "gathering the joys of long life" — finished the next year.

In 1588 he received Emperor Go-Yōzei there and had the lords swear loyalty to him before the emperor; an imperial visit proclaimed him master of the realm.

Hideyoshi later handed the Jurakudai to his nephew and heir, the regent Toyotomi Hidetsugu. But in 1595 — Hideyoshi now had a son of his own, Hideyori — Hidetsugu was accused of treason and made to kill himself, and the Jurakudai was razed without a trace. Its glory lasted eight years.

title.en: The Great Buddha of Kyoto and the bell inscription

body.ja:
豊臣秀吉は1586年、京の東山に、奈良の大仏をしのぐ大仏殿を建て始めた。刀狩で集めた刀を釘や鎹にする、と言って百姓から武器を取り上げたのは、この大仏のためであった。

大仏は1595年に完成したが、翌年の大地震で壊れた。秀吉の死後、子の秀頼が再建に取りかかり、1614年に大きな鐘を鋳た。その銘に「国家安康」「君臣豊楽」の句があった。

[[p:徳川家康]]の側は、これを「家康」の名を二つに切って呪い、「豊臣」を君として楽しむ意図だと咎めた。豊臣方の弁明は聞き入れられず、これが大坂冬の陣の口実となった。鐘は今も京都に残り、問題の句は白く囲まれて見ることができる。
body.en:
In 1586 Toyotomi Hideyoshi began a Great Buddha hall in eastern Kyoto to outdo the Great Buddha of Nara; it was for this Buddha, he said, that the sword hunt took the farmers' blades to make nails and clamps.

The image was finished in 1595 and wrecked by a great earthquake the next year. After Hideyoshi's death his son Hideyori rebuilt it, and in 1614 cast a great bell. Its inscription included the phrases "May the state be peaceful and secure" and "lord and vassal rejoice in plenty".

[[p:徳川家康|Tokugawa Ieyasu]]'s side took offence: the first, they said, cut the characters of "Ieyasu" in two as a curse, and the second hailed the Toyotomi as lords. The Toyotomi explanations were not heard, and the bell became the pretext for the winter campaign at Osaka. The bell still hangs in Kyoto, the offending phrases outlined in white.

body.ja:
北条家の本拠小田原城は、[[p:上杉謙信]]や[[p:武田信玄]]の大軍に囲まれても落ちなかった堅城である。豊臣秀吉との戦いが近づくと、北条家は1587年から、城だけでなく城下町と田畑まで丸ごと囲む堀と土塁「総構」を築いた。周囲はおよそ九キロに及んだ。

1590年、秀吉は二十万を超える大軍で小田原を囲んだ。北条家は総構に籠もって長期戦を構えたが、秀吉は城を見下ろす石垣山に、わずか八十日ほどで石垣の城を築き、完成すると周りの木を一斉に切り払って、一夜で城が現れたように見せた (石垣山一夜城)。

城内では降伏か籠城かの評定が延々と続き、なかなか決まらなかった。「小田原評定」という言葉はここから生まれたという。三か月の籠城ののち、北条家は城を開き、五代百年の歴史を閉じた。
body.en:
Odawara, the Hōjō seat, had held even against the great armies of [[p:上杉謙信|Uesugi Kenshin]] and [[p:武田信玄|Takeda Shingen]]. As war with Toyotomi Hideyoshi loomed, from 1587 the Hōjō ringed not only the castle but the whole town and its fields with a moat and earth rampart — the sōgamae — some nine kilometres around.

In 1590 Hideyoshi surrounded Odawara with more than two hundred thousand men. The Hōjō settled in for a long siege. On Mount Ishigaki overlooking the castle, Hideyoshi built a stone-walled castle in some eighty days, then cut down the trees in front of it all at once so that it seemed to appear overnight — the "one-night castle".

Inside, council after council debated surrender or resistance and could decide nothing — "an Odawara council" became a byword for endless talk. After three months the Hōjō opened the gates, and five generations and a century of their house came to an end.

title.en: Edo castle and the national works

body.ja:
1590年、関東へ移された[[p:徳川家康]]は、本拠を小田原ではなく、入江に面した小さな城と寒村の江戸に置いた。家臣たちを驚かせたこの選択は、水運と広い平野を見込んだものであった。

1603年に将軍となった家康は、全国の大名に命じて江戸城と城下町の工事を分担させた (天下普請)。伊豆の石を船で運び、神田の山を崩して入江を埋め立て、町を造った。1607年には五層の天守が完成した。

天下普請は、大名の財を削いで力を弱める意味もあった。江戸は、のちに人口百万を超える世界有数の都市となっていく。
body.en:
Moved to the Kantō in 1590, [[p:徳川家康|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] made his seat not at Odawara but at Edo, a small castle and a poor village on an inlet — a choice that startled his men, made with an eye on water transport and the wide plain.

Shogun from 1603, Ieyasu had the lords of the whole country share the work on Edo castle and its town — the "national works". Stone came by ship from Izu; the Kanda hills were cut down to fill in the inlet for the town. In 1607 a five-storey keep was finished.

The national works also drained the lords' purses and so their power. Edo grew into one of the great cities of the world, with more than a million people.

body.ja:
播磨の姫路城は、[[p:羽柴秀吉]]が中国攻めの拠点として三層の天守を築いた城である。関ヶ原の後、[[p:徳川家康]]の娘婿池田輝政が播磨を与えられ、1601年から九年をかけて大きな城に造り替えた。

白漆喰で塗り込めた大天守と三つの小天守が渡り廊下でつながる姿は、羽を広げた白鷺にたとえられ、「白鷺城」と呼ばれる。迷路のように曲がりくねった道、多くの門と狭間は、攻め手を惑わせ、横から撃てるように工夫されている。

姫路城は、西国の大名ににらみを利かせる徳川方の要であった。戦にも火事にも遭わず、江戸時代の天守を今に残す城として、世界の遺産となっている。
body.en:
Himeji in Harima was the castle where [[p:羽柴秀吉|Hashiba Hideyoshi]] built a three-storey keep as his base for the western campaigns. After Sekigahara [[p:徳川家康|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave Harima to his son-in-law Ikeda Terumasa, who spent nine years from 1601 rebuilding it on a grand scale.

Its great keep and three smaller keeps, plastered white and joined by covered passages, are likened to a white heron spreading its wings — "the White Heron Castle". Its winding maze of paths and many gates and loopholes were laid out to confuse attackers and shoot them from the side.

Himeji was a Tokugawa stronghold watching the lords of the west. Spared by war and fire, it keeps its keep of the age to this day, a heritage of the world.

body.ja:
[[p:今川義元]]は二万五千と号する大軍で尾張へ入り、松平元康 (家康) らに大高城・鷲津・丸根の砦を攻めさせた。義元の本隊五千ほどは桶狭間の山あいで休息していた。[[p:織田信長]]は清洲から二千ほどで出た。

信長は夜明けに「敦盛」を舞って出陣し、熱田神宮で兵を集めた。砦が落ちたとの知らせを受けながら、善照寺砦から中島砦へ進み、昼過ぎの激しい雷雨の中を今川本隊に向かって突き進んだ。雨が上がった瞬間に襲いかかられた本隊は崩れ、義元は毛利新介に討たれた。

「人間五十年、下天のうちをくらぶれば、夢幻のごとくなり」。出陣の朝、信長は幸若舞「敦盛」のこの一節を舞い、湯漬けをかき込んで、わずかな供と城を飛び出したという。

義元を討った毛利新介は、首を取るとき義元に指を食いちぎられたと伝わる。

今川家は大きく揺らぎ、松平元康は岡崎で自立した。信長の名は一夜で天下に知られた。

兵力 (目安): 3,000 対 25,000。損害: 800 対 3,000。
body.en:
[[p:今川義元|Imagawa Yoshimoto]] entered Owari with a host said to number twenty-five thousand, and set [[p:まつ|Matsu]]daira Motoyasu (Ieyasu) and others against the Ōdaka castle and the forts of Washizu and Marune. Yoshimoto's own column, five thousand or so, rested in the hollows of Okehazama. [[p:織田信長|Oda Nobunaga]] rode out of Kiyosu with about two thousand.

Nobunaga danced "Atsumori" at dawn and rode out, gathering his men at the Atsuta shrine. Hearing the forts had fallen, he pushed on from Zenshōji to Nakajima and, in a violent thunderstorm after noon, drove straight at the Imagawa column. It broke the moment the rain stopped and he fell on it; Yoshimoto was cut down by Mōri Shinsuke.

"Fifty years of a man's life, beside the realm below heaven, are a dream, an illusion." On the morning he rode out Nobunaga danced these lines from the ballad Atsumori, gulped a bowl of rice in hot water and dashed from the castle with a handful of men.

Mōri Shinsuke, who killed Yoshimoto, is said to have lost a finger, bitten off by Yoshimoto as he took his head.

The Imagawa house was shaken to its roots and Matsudaira Motoyasu made himself independent at Okazaki. Overnight Nobunaga's name was known throughout the land.

Troops (rough): 3,000 against 25,000. Losses: 800 against 3,000.

body.ja:
[[p:上杉謙信]]は妻女山に陣取り、[[p:武田信玄]]は海津城に入った。武田は兵を二つに分け、[[p:高坂昌信]]・[[p:馬場信春]]らの別働隊一万二千が妻女山を背後から突き、信玄の本隊八千が八幡原で待ち受けることにした。

[[p:山本勘助]]の「啄木鳥の戦法」(木をつついて飛び出した虫を食う) であったが、謙信は海津城から上がる炊煙の多さで動きを見抜き、夜のうちに山を下りて霧の八幡原に陣を敷いた。霧が晴れると、目の前に上杉の全軍がいた。上杉は「車懸り」で次々と新手を繰り出し、武田の本隊は崩れかけたが、別働隊が駆けつけて上杉を挟んだ。

白い頭巾の騎馬武者がただ一騎、信玄の本陣に斬り込み、床几に座る信玄に三太刀を浴びせた。信玄は軍配で受け止めたと伝わる (一騎討ちは後の軍記の語るところ)。

信玄の弟[[p:武田信繁]]と軍師山本勘助は、この戦いで討死した。信繁の家訓は、のちの武士の手本とされた。

両軍とも多くを失い、勝敗ははっきりしなかった。北信濃は武田のものとして残った。

兵力 (目安): 20,000 対 13,000。損害: 4,000 対 3,400。
body.en:
[[p:上杉謙信|Uesugi Kenshin]] camped on Mount Saijo; [[p:武田信玄|Takeda Shingen]] entered Kaizu castle. Takeda split his army: a detachment of twelve thousand under [[p:高坂昌信|Kōsaka Masanobu]] and [[p:馬場信春|Baba Nobuharu]] would strike the mountain from behind, while Shingen's main body of eight thousand waited on the plain of Hachimanbara.

It was [[p:山本勘助|Yamamoto Kansuke]]'s "woodpecker" plan — peck at the tree and catch the insects that fly out. But Kenshin read it from the many cooking fires smoking over Kaizu, came down the mountain by night and drew up in the fog on Hachimanbara. When the fog lifted, Shingen found the whole Uesugi army before him. The Uesugi sent in fresh troops wave on wave; the Takeda main body was close to breaking when the detachment arrived and caught the Uesugi between them.

A horseman in a white hood rode alone into Shingen's camp and slashed three times at Shingen on his stool, who caught the blows on his war fan — so the later war tales tell.

Shingen's brother [[p:武田信繁|Takeda Nobushige]] and his strategist Yamamoto Kansuke were killed in the battle; Nobushige's house rules were later held up as a model for warriors.

Both sides lost heavily and neither clearly won; northern Shinano stayed Takeda land.

Troops (rough): 20,000 against 13,000. Losses: 4,000 against 3,400.

title.en: the battle of the Ane river

body.ja:
織田・徳川の連合軍は姉川の南に陣し、北岸に浅井・朝倉の連合軍が並んだ。徳川は朝倉、織田は浅井と向き合った。

浅井の磯野員昌は織田の陣を十三段のうち十一段まで突き崩したと伝わる。だが徳川勢が朝倉を押し返し、[[p:榊原康政]]が横から朝倉を突いて崩すと、浅井も支えきれずに退いた。

姉川の水は血で赤く染まり、のちに「血原」「血川」と呼ばれる地名が残ったという。

浅井・朝倉は敗れたものの滅びず、本願寺や武田と結んで信長を包囲していく。

兵力 (目安): 28,000 対 13,000。損害: 800 対 3,000。
body.en:
Oda and Tokugawa drew up south of the Ane; Azai and Asakura faced them on the north bank. Tokugawa took on Asakura, Oda the Azai.

Isono Kazumasa of the Azai is said to have broken eleven of the thirteen lines of the Oda array. But the Tokugawa pushed the Asakura back, [[p:榊原康政|Sakakibara Yasumasa]] took them in the flank, and when the Asakura broke the Azai could not hold either.

The waters of the Ane ran red, and places there were called "the Field of Blood" and "the River of Blood" ever after, they say.

Azai and Asakura were beaten but not destroyed; with the Ishiyama believers and the Takeda they went on to encircle Nobunaga.

Troops (rough): 28,000 against 13,000. Losses: 800 against 3,000.

body.ja:
西へ進む[[p:武田信玄]]の大軍は、浜松城を素通りして三方ヶ原の台地へ上がった。家康は織田の援軍を合わせ一万一千で城を出て、背後を襲おうとした。

武田は台地の上で振り返り、「魚鱗」の陣で待ち受けていた。家康は横に広い「鶴翼」で挑んだが、夕暮れから二時間ほどで崩れ、浜松城へ逃げ戻った。

城に戻った家康は、門を開けたままかがり火を焚かせた (空城の計)。追ってきた[[p:山県昌景]]は罠を疑って引き返したという。

家康はこの敗戦の苦い顔を絵師に描かせ、慢心の戒めとしたと伝わる (いわゆる「しかみ像」。この由来は後世の言い伝えともいう)。

信玄はそのまま西へ進んだが、翌年の春に病に倒れ、甲斐へ帰る途中で世を去った。

兵力 (目安): 27,000 対 11,000。損害: 200 対 2,000。
body.en:
Shingen's great army marched west past Hamamatsu castle and climbed onto the Mikatagahara plateau. Ieyasu came out with eleven thousand, Oda reinforcements included, to fall on its rear.

On the plateau the Takeda turned and waited in a "fish scale" wedge. Ieyasu came on in a wide "crane's wing" and in two hours of dusk was broken and fled back to Hamamatsu.

Back in the castle Ieyasu had the gates left open and bonfires lit; pursuing, [[p:山県昌景|Yamagata Masakage]] suspected a trap and turned back, it is said.

Ieyasu is said to have had a painter draw his face twisted with the bitterness of this defeat, as a warning against pride — though the story behind the portrait may be a later tradition.

Shingen marched on west, but fell ill the next spring and died on the way home to Kai.

Troops (rough): 27,000 against 11,000. Losses: 200 against 2,000.

body.ja:
[[p:武田勝頼]]は長篠城を囲んだ。救援に来た織田・徳川は設楽原の連吾川沿いに陣を敷き、川の手前に二重三重の馬防柵を築いた。

織田の[[p:酒井忠次]]の別働隊が夜のうちに鳶ノ巣山砦を奪い、武田は背後を断たれた。勝頼は決戦を選び、[[p:山県昌景]]らの軍勢が柵に向かって次々と攻めかかったが、柵の内から撃ちかけられる多数の鉄砲と弓に阻まれた。昼過ぎまでに武田の名将の多くが討たれた。

「鉄砲三千挺の三段撃ち」は後世の軍記が広めた話で、実際の数や撃ち方ははっきりしない。それでも多くの鉄砲を柵とともに使ったことは確かとされる。

長篠城では、援軍を求めて城を抜け出した鳥居強右衛門が武田に捕らえられ、「援軍は来ない」と城に叫ぶよう命じられた。彼は「援軍はすぐ来る」と叫び、磔にされた。

武田は山県・馬場・内藤らを失い、急速に力を落とした。七年後、武田家は滅ぶ。

兵力 (目安): 38,000 対 15,000。損害: 600 対 10,000。
body.en:
[[p:武田勝頼|Takeda Katsuyori]] besieged Nagashino castle. The Oda and Tokugawa came to relieve it and drew up along the Rengo stream at Shitaragahara, building double and triple palisades against horse in front of it.

A detachment under [[p:酒井忠次|Sakai Tadatsugu]] took the Tobinosuyama fort by night, cutting the Takeda off behind. Katsuyori chose battle; [[p:山県昌景|Yamagata Masakage]] and the rest charged the palisades wave after wave, and were stopped by the guns and bows firing from behind them. By early afternoon most of Takeda's great captains were dead.

"Three thousand guns firing in three ranks" is a tale spread by later war chronicles; the true numbers and drill are uncertain. That many guns were used together with the palisades is beyond doubt.

At Nagashino castle, Torii Suneemon slipped out to fetch help, was caught by the Takeda and ordered to shout to the castle that no help was coming. He shouted that help was near, and was crucified.

Takeda lost Yamagata, Baba, Naitō and many more, and its strength drained away; seven years later the house was gone.

Troops (rough): 38,000 against 15,000. Losses: 600 against 10,000.

title.en: the battle of the Mimi river

body.ja:
[[p:大友宗麟]]は日向に大軍を送り、島津方の高城を囲ませた。[[p:島津義久]]は救援に向かい、高城川 (小丸川) を挟んで大友軍と対した。

功を焦る[[p:田北鎮周]]が川を渡って攻めかかると、島津は少数の囮を退かせ、伏せていた左右の兵で包み込んだ (釣り野伏せ)。崩れた大友軍は耳川まで追われ、増水した川で多くが溺れた。

大友軍の将たちは仲が悪く、総大将の[[p:田原紹忍]]は戦いの最中も采配が定まらなかったという。

大友は多くの重臣を失い、島津は九州の覇権を目指して北上する。

兵力 (目安): 30,000 対 43,000。損害: 3,000 対 20,000。
body.en:
[[p:大友宗麟|Ōtomo Sōrin]] sent a great army into Hyūga to besiege the Shimazu castle of Taka; [[p:島津義久|Shimazu Yoshihisa]] came to its aid and faced the Ōtomo across the Takajō river.

The impatient [[p:田北鎮周|Tagita Shigekane]] crossed and attacked; the Shimazu let a small decoy fall back and closed on the pursuers with men hidden on both sides — the "fishing ambush". The broken Ōtomo army was chased to the Mimi river, where many drowned in the flood.

The Ōtomo generals were at odds, and their commander [[p:田原紹忍|Tawara Jōnin]] could not settle on orders even as the battle went on.

Ōtomo lost many of its leading men; the Shimazu turned north, aiming for mastery of Kyūshū.

Troops (rough): 30,000 against 43,000. Losses: 3,000 against 20,000.

body.ja:
[[p:龍造寺隆信]]は[[p:有馬晴信]]を攻めた。[[p:島津家久]]はわずかな兵で有馬を助け、湿地の中を細い畷 (あぜ道) が通る沖田に陣を敷いた。

大軍の龍造寺勢は細い道に縦長に伸び、湿地に足を取られた。島津は囮で誘い込み、左右の茂みから鉄砲と弓で撃ちかけて斬り込んだ。乱戦の中で隆信は討たれた。

肥満で馬に乗れなかった隆信は、六人担ぎの輿に乗って戦場に出ていたと伝わる。

龍造寺は島津に従い、九州は島津・大友の争いとなった。

兵力 (目安): 6,000 対 25,000。損害: 250 対 3,000。
body.en:
[[p:龍造寺隆信|Ryūzōji Takanobu]] marched on [[p:有馬晴信|Arima Harunobu]]. [[p:島津家久|Shimazu Iehisa]] came to Arima's aid with a small force and took his stand at Okita, where narrow causeways ran through the marsh.

The great Ryūzōji army stretched thin along the narrow paths and bogged down in the marsh. The Shimazu drew it in with a decoy and struck from the thickets on both sides with guns and bows, then swords. In the melee Takanobu was killed.

Takanobu, too stout to ride, is said to have gone into battle in a palanquin carried by six men.

Ryūzōji bowed to the Shimazu, and Kyūshū was left to Shimazu and Ōtomo.

Troops (rough): 6,000 against 25,000. Losses: 250 against 3,000.

body.ja:
織田信雄と結んだ家康は小牧山に陣を構え、秀吉は大軍で対した。両軍とも砦を築いて睨み合った。

[[p:池田恒興]]らは手薄な家康の本国三河を突く「中入り」を進言し、二万の別働隊が動いた。家康はこれを察してひそかに追い、長久手で別働隊を破って池田恒興と森長可を討ち取った。

[[p:井伊直政]]の部隊は甲冑を赤一色に揃えた「赤備え」で、敵に恐れられたという。

秀吉は戦いでは勝てなかったが、信雄と単独で和を結んで家康の大義名分を奪った。家康はのちに秀吉に臣従する。

兵力 (目安): 16,000 対 60,000。損害: 600 対 2,500。
body.en:
Allied with Oda Nobukatsu, Ieyasu fortified Mount Komaki; Hideyoshi faced him with a far larger army, and both sides dug in behind their forts.

[[p:池田恒興|Ikeda Tsuneoki]] proposed a raid deep into Ieyasu's home province of Mikawa, and a detachment of twenty thousand set out. Ieyasu saw it, followed in secret, and destroyed it at Nagakute, killing Ikeda Tsuneoki and Mori Nagayoshi.

[[p:井伊直政|Ii Naomasa]]'s men wore armour all in red — the "red guard" — and their enemies dreaded them.

Hideyoshi could not win in the field, but made a separate peace with Nobukatsu and took away Ieyasu's cause; Ieyasu later bowed to him.

Troops (rough): 16,000 against 60,000. Losses: 600 against 2,500.

body.ja:
[[p:伊達政宗]]は磐梯山の麓、摺上原で[[p:蘆名義広]]と戦った。初めは向かい風に砂塵を浴びて苦しんだが、風向きが変わると攻勢に転じ、蘆名勢を日橋川へ追い落とした。

蘆名家中には政宗に内通した者が多く、戦いの最中に兵を動かさない家臣もいたという。

政宗は会津を得て南奥州の大半を手にしたが、翌年の小田原征伐に遅参し、秀吉に会津を取り上げられる。

兵力 (目安): 23,000 対 16,000。損害: 300 対 1,800。
body.en:
[[p:伊達政宗|Date Masamune]] met [[p:蘆名義広|Ashina Yoshihiro]] at Suriagehara under Mount Bandai. At first the wind drove dust into his men's faces; when it turned, he went over to the attack and drove the Ashina into the Nippashi river.

Many in the Ashina house were secretly in touch with Masamune, and some of its men never moved during the battle.

Masamune won Aizu and most of southern Ōu — and the next year, late to the siege of Odawara, lost Aizu to Hideyoshi.

Troops (rough): 23,000 against 16,000. Losses: 300 against 1,800.

body.ja:
西軍は[[p:石田三成]]・[[p:宇喜多秀家]]・[[p:小西行長]]・[[p:大谷吉継]]らが関ヶ原の西に陣を敷き、南の松尾山に[[p:小早川秀秋]]、東の南宮山に毛利秀元・吉川広家らが陣取って、東軍を包み込む形をとった。東軍は[[p:福島正則]]を先鋒に、家康は桃配山に本陣を置いた。

朝の霧の中、[[p:井伊直政]]の抜け駆けで戦いが始まった。西軍は善戦し、昼まで一進一退が続いた。毛利勢は吉川広家が東軍と通じていて動かず、松尾山の小早川秀秋も動かなかった。昼過ぎ、家康が松尾山に鉄砲を撃ちかけると (問鉄砲。後世の話ともいう)、秀秋は東軍に寝返って大谷吉継の陣に攻め下った。脇坂ら四将も寝返り、西軍は総崩れとなった。

病で目が見えなくなっていた大谷吉継は、寝返りを予期して備えていたが支えきれず自害した。親友の石田三成の頼みで、負けを承知で西軍に加わっていたという。

[[p:島津義弘]]は敵中を正面突破して退却した (島津の退き口)。甥の豊久らが次々と殿に残って討たれ、千五百の兵のうち薩摩に帰り着いたのは数十人であったという。

捕らえられた三成は、処刑の前に喉が渇いて湯を求め、代わりに干し柿を勧められると「痰の毒だ」と断った。「大志を抱く者は最期まで命を惜しむ」と言ったという。

戦いは一日で終わり、家康は西軍の大名の領地を取り上げて味方に分け与えた。三年後、家康は征夷大将軍となる。

兵力 (目安): 75,000 対 80,000。損害: 4,000 対 8,000。
body.en:
The western army — [[p:石田三成|Ishida Mitsunari]], [[p:宇喜多秀家|Ukita Hideie]], [[p:小西行長|Konishi Yukinaga]], [[p:大谷吉継|Ōtani Yoshitsugu]] and others — drew up on the west side of Sekigahara, with [[p:小早川秀秋|Kobayakawa Hideaki]] on Mount [[p:まつ|Matsu]]o to the south and Mōri Hidemoto and Kikkawa Hiroie on Mount Nangū to the east, as if to enfold the eastern army. The east sent [[p:福島正則|Fukushima Masanori]] forward; Ieyasu set his headquarters on Mount Momokubari.

In the morning fog [[p:井伊直政|Ii Naomasa]] jumped the start and the battle began. The west fought well, and until noon neither side gave way. The Mōri did not move — Kikkawa Hiroie had a secret understanding with the east — and neither did Kobayakawa on Mount Matsuo. After noon Ieyasu had guns fired at the mountain (a later story, some say); Hideaki went over to the east and charged down on Ōtani Yoshitsugu. Four more commanders turned, and the western army collapsed.

Ōtani Yoshitsugu, half blind with illness, had foreseen the betrayal and prepared for it, but could not hold, and took his own life. He had joined the west knowing it would lose, they say, because his friend Ishida Mitsunari asked him.

[[p:島津義弘|Shimazu Yoshihiro]] retreated by cutting straight through the enemy — "the Shimazu withdrawal". His nephew Toyohisa and others stayed behind one after another to hold the pursuers and died; of fifteen hundred men only a few dozen reached Satsuma.

Captured, Mitsunari asked for hot water before his execution; offered a dried persimmon instead, he refused it as bad for the phlegm. "A man with great aims guards his life to the end," he said.

The battle was over in a day. Ieyasu stripped the western daimyo of their lands and handed them to his own side; three years later he was shogun.

Troops (rough): 75,000 against 80,000. Losses: 4,000 against 8,000.

body.ja:
冬の陣の和議で堀を埋められた大坂城は守れず、豊臣方は城を出て天王寺・岡山口に陣を敷いた。家康は天王寺口、秀忠は岡山口から攻めた。

[[p:真田信繁]]は天王寺口から家康の本陣めがけて突撃し、三度にわたって斬り込んで本陣の旗を倒した。家康は一時、自害を覚悟したとも伝わる。だが数に勝る徳川勢が押し返し、信繁は安居神社で討たれた。城には火が放たれた。

真田信繁を敵方の島津家の記録は「日本一の兵」と讃えた。

秀頼と[[p:淀殿]]は山里曲輪の蔵に籠もり、助命の願いが聞き入れられないと知って自害した。

豊臣家は滅び、元号は元和と改められた。応仁の乱から続いた戦乱の世は終わった。

兵力 (目安): 155,000 対 55,000。損害: 10,000 対 20,000。
body.en:
With its moats filled in after the winter peace, Osaka castle could not be held; the Toyotomi side came out and drew up at Tennōji and Okayama. Ieyasu attacked at Tennōji, Hidetada at Okayama.

[[p:真田信繁|Sanada Nobushige]] charged from Tennōji straight at Ieyasu's headquarters, broke in three times and brought down its standard; Ieyasu, some say, was ready to kill himself. But the larger Tokugawa army pushed back, and Nobushige was killed at the Yasui shrine. The castle was set on fire.

The records of the Shimazu, on the other side, called Sanada Nobushige "the finest soldier in Japan".

Hideyori and [[p:淀殿|Lady Yodo]] shut themselves in a storehouse in the inner citadel, and when they learned no mercy would be given, took their own lives.

The house of Toyotomi was gone and the era was renamed Genna. The age of war that had begun with the Ōnin war was over.

Troops (rough): 155,000 against 55,000. Losses: 10,000 against 20,000.

body.ja:
1561年、第四次川中島の戦いで、武田の軍師[[p:山本勘助]]が立てたと伝わる策。啄木鳥は木の幹をくちばしでつついて、驚いて穴から出てきた虫を食べる。それにならって、別働隊が妻女山の上杉軍を背後からつつき、山を下りてきたところを本隊が八幡原で待ち受けて討つ、というものであった。

だが[[p:上杉謙信]]は、海津城から立ちのぼる炊事の煙がいつもより多いのを見て、武田が夜に動くと見抜いた。謙信は夜のうちにひそかに山を下り、千曲川を渡った。「鞭声粛々夜河を過る」——のちの漢詩人頼山陽がこの場面をそう詠んでいる。

朝霧が晴れたとき、八幡原の武田本隊の目の前には、上杉の全軍が陣を敷いていた。勘助は策が破れた責めを負うように敵中に斬り込み、討死したと伝わる。もっとも、山本勘助の実在そのものが長く疑われていた (近年、実在を示す手紙が見つかっている)。
body.en:
The plan said to have been devised by the Takeda strategist [[p:山本勘助|Yamamoto Kansuke]] at the fourth battle of Kawanakajima in 1561. A woodpecker taps the trunk and eats the insects that scurry out; so a detachment would strike the Uesugi on Mount Saijo from behind, and the main army would wait for them on the plain of Hachimanbara as they came down.

But [[p:上杉謙信|Uesugi Kenshin]] saw more cooking smoke than usual rising from Kaizu castle and guessed the Takeda would move by night. He slipped down the mountain in the dark and crossed the Chikuma river — "whips silent, by night we crossed the river," as the later poet Rai San'yō wrote of it.

When the morning fog lifted, the Takeda main body on Hachimanbara found the whole Uesugi army drawn up in front of it. Kansuke, it is said, charged into the enemy as if to atone and was killed — though whether he existed at all was long doubted (letters naming him have since been found).

body.ja:
九州の島津家が得意とした戦法。兵を三つに分け、二つを左右に伏せておく。中央の囮の部隊が敵とぶつかったのち、負けたふりをして退く。勢いに乗って追ってきた敵を、伏せていた左右の兵と、向き直った中央の兵が三方から包んで討つ。餌で魚を釣り上げるように敵を誘い出すことから「釣り野伏せ」と呼ばれた。

島津家はこの戦法で、耳川で大友の大軍を、沖田畷で龍造寺の大軍を破った。数で劣っても勝てるのは、囮の部隊が崩れずに退く難しさをこなせる、鍛えられた兵がいたからである。

関ヶ原の退き口でも、島津は「捨て奸」と呼ばれる、少数が踏みとどまって死ぬまで戦う殿の戦法で追っ手を食い止めた。
body.en:
The trademark tactic of the Shimazu of Kyūshū. The army was split in three, two parts hidden on the flanks. The centre, a decoy, engaged and then fell back as if beaten; when the enemy pursued, the hidden wings and the turning centre closed on it from three sides. Luring the enemy out like a fish on a line gave it its name.

With it the Shimazu broke the great Ōtomo army at the Mimi river and the great Ryūzōji army at Okitanawate. Winning with fewer men took troops drilled to retreat without breaking — the hardest part.

In the Shimazu retreat at Sekigahara, small parties stayed behind to fight to the death and hold the pursuers — "sutegamari".

body.ja:
関ヶ原で西軍が総崩れになったとき、[[p:島津義弘]]の軍はわずか千五百ほどで、敵中に取り残された。後ろは伊吹山、まわりは東軍。義弘は前へ——家康の本陣のすぐ横をかすめて、敵中を正面から突破して退くことを選んだ。

追う[[p:井伊直政]]や[[p:本多忠勝]]の軍に、甥の島津豊久らが次々と踏みとどまって戦い、死んでいった。井伊直政はこの追撃で鉄砲に撃たれて傷を負い、それがもとでのちに世を去ったという。

義弘が薩摩に帰り着いたとき、従う者は数十人であった。だがこの勇名は、のちに島津家が領地を減らされずに済むことにもつながった。
body.en:
When the western army collapsed at Sekigahara, [[p:島津義弘|Shimazu Yoshihiro]] was left in the midst of the enemy with some fifteen hundred men, Mount Ibuki behind and the eastern army all around. He chose to go forward — straight through the enemy, past the very flank of Ieyasu's headquarters.

As [[p:井伊直政|Ii Naomasa]] and [[p:本多忠勝|Honda Tadakatsu]] pursued, his nephew Shimazu Toyohisa and others stayed behind one after another, fought and died. Ii Naomasa was wounded by a gunshot in the chase and later died of it, they say.

When Yoshihiro reached Satsuma only a few dozen were with him. But the fame of it helped the Shimazu keep their lands undiminished afterwards.

body.ja:
1614年、大坂冬の陣。大坂城は北・西・東を川や堀に守られていたが、南だけは平地が続いて弱かった。[[p:真田信繁]]はそこに、半月形の出丸を築いた。のちに「真田丸」と呼ばれる砦である。

十二月、徳川方の前田・井伊・松平らの軍が真田丸に攻め寄せた。信繁は挑発して敵を空堀に誘い込み、塀の内から鉄砲を浴びせた。攻め手は数千の死傷者を出して退いた。

和議の後、真田丸は真っ先に壊された。夏の陣で信繁は家康の本陣に三度斬り込んで討死し、敵方からも「日本一の兵」と讃えられた。のちの講談や小説では「真田幸村」の名で、真田十勇士とともに活躍する英雄となる。
body.en:
Winter, 1614. Osaka castle was guarded by rivers and moats to the north, west and east, but to the south flat ground ran right up to it. [[p:真田信繁|Sanada Nobushige]] built a half-moon outwork there — later called the Sanada-maru.

In December the Tokugawa armies of Maeda, Ii and [[p:まつ|Matsu]]daira stormed it. Nobushige taunted them into the dry moat and poured gunfire on them from behind the walls; the attackers fell back having lost thousands.

After the peace the Sanada-maru was the first thing pulled down. In the summer siege Nobushige charged Ieyasu's headquarters three times and was killed, praised even by his enemies as "the finest soldier in Japan". Later storytellers and novels made him "Sanada Yukimura", hero of the Ten Braves of Sanada.

body.ja:
1567年、[[p:今川氏真]]は[[p:北条氏康]]と結んで、甲斐の[[p:武田信玄]]への塩の道を止めた。海のない甲斐と信濃は、塩を外から運ばなければならない。

このとき越後の[[p:上杉謙信]]は、宿敵の信玄に塩を送ったと伝わる。「争うところは弓矢にあり、米や塩ではない」と言ったという。実際には塩を送ったというより、越後の商人に甲斐への塩の商いを止めさせなかった、というのが近い姿だとも言われる。

この話から、苦しい立場の敵を助けることを「敵に塩を送る」と言うようになった。信玄は死の床で、子の勝頼に「謙信を頼れ」と言い残したとも伝わる。
body.en:
In 1567 [[p:今川氏真|Imagawa Ujizane]], with [[p:北条氏康|Hōjō Ujiyasu]], cut the salt roads into the lands of [[p:武田信玄|Takeda Shingen]]. Landlocked Kai and Shinano had to bring in their salt.

[[p:上杉謙信|Uesugi Kenshin]] of Echigo, his great rival, is said to have sent Shingen salt: "We fight with bows and arrows, not with rice and salt." In fact he probably just did not stop Echigo merchants from selling salt to Kai.

So "sending salt to an enemy" came to mean helping a foe in his hour of need. On his deathbed, they say, Shingen told his son Katsuyori to rely on Kenshin.

body.ja:
[[p:毛利元就]]は死の床に三人の子、隆元・[[p:吉川元春]]・[[p:小早川隆景]]を呼び、一本の矢を折らせた。矢はたやすく折れた。次に三本を束ねて折らせると、誰も折れなかった。「三人が力を合わせれば、毛利家は誰にも負けない」。

もっとも、隆元は元就より先に亡くなっているので、この話は後世の作り話と考えられている。もとになったのは、元就が1557年に三人に送った長い手紙「三子教訓状」である。そこには、兄弟が仲良くし、毛利の家を第一に考えるよう、くどいほど書かれていた。

吉川と小早川の「両川」は兄を支え、元就の死後も毛利家を守った。サッカーのチーム名や、町おこしの合言葉にもなっている。
body.en:
On his deathbed, the story goes, [[p:毛利元就|Mōri Motonari]] called his three sons — Takamoto, [[p:吉川元春|Kikkawa Motoharu]] and [[p:小早川隆景|Kobayakawa Takakage]] — and had them break a single arrow, which snapped easily; then three bound together, which none could break. "If the three of you stand together, no one can defeat the Mōri."

But Takamoto died before his father, so the story is thought to be a later invention. It grew from the long letter Motonari wrote to the three in 1557, urging them over and over to keep the peace among themselves and put the house of Mōri first.

The "two rivers" — Kikkawa and Kobayakawa — upheld their brother and kept the Mōri safe after Motonari's death. The arrows now name a football club and a hundred local campaigns.

title.ja: 鳴かぬなら……ほととぎす
title.en: If the cuckoo will not sing

body.ja:
三人の天下人の性格を、ほととぎすで言い表した句が知られている。[[p:織田信長]]は「鳴かぬなら殺してしまえほととぎす」、豊臣秀吉は「鳴かぬなら鳴かせてみせようほととぎす」、[[p:徳川家康]]は「鳴かぬなら鳴くまで待とうほととぎす」。

これは本人たちが詠んだものではなく、江戸時代の随筆に載る後世の人のたとえである。苛烈な信長、才覚の秀吉、忍耐の家康——人々の抱いた三人の姿をよく表している。

同じように、「織田がつき、羽柴がこねし天下餅、座りしままに食うは徳川」という狂歌もある。信長が餅をつき、秀吉がこね、座ったまま食べたのは家康だ、というのである。
body.en:
A famous trio of verses sums up the three unifiers through a cuckoo that will not sing. Nobunaga: "If it will not sing — kill it." Hideyoshi: "If it will not sing — I will make it sing." Ieyasu: "If it will not sing — I will wait until it does."

They wrote nothing of the kind; the verses appear in an Edo-period miscellany. But they catch how people saw the three: fierce Nobunaga, resourceful Hideyoshi, patient Ieyasu.

A comic verse makes the same point: "Oda pounded the rice cake of the realm, Hashiba kneaded it, and Tokugawa, never rising from his seat, ate it."

body.ja:
1570年、越前の朝倉を攻めて金ヶ崎城まで進んだ[[p:織田信長]]のもとに、妹[[p:お市]]の夫[[p:浅井長政]]が背いたという知らせが届いた。前に朝倉、後ろに浅井。挟み撃ちの危機である。お市が両端を縛った小豆の袋を兄に送って知らせた、という話も伝わる (後世の話ともいう)。

信長はただちに全軍を置いて、わずかな供と琵琶湖の西の朽木谷を抜けて京へ逃げ帰った。最も危険な殿 (しんがり) を引き受けたのが、木下藤吉郎 (秀吉) であり、[[p:明智光秀]]や[[p:徳川家康]]も加わったとされる。

殿の軍は追いすがる朝倉勢を防ぎながら退き、信長は生き延びた。この働きで秀吉の名は大いに上がった。
body.en:
In 1570, having advanced against the Asakura of Echizen as far as Kanegasaki, [[p:織田信長|Oda Nobunaga]] learned that [[p:浅井長政|Azai Nagamasa]], husband of his sister [[p:お市|Oichi]], had turned against him: the Asakura ahead, the Azai behind. Oichi, the story goes, warned her brother with a bag of beans tied at both ends — though that may be a later tale.

Nobunaga left the army at once and fled back to Kyoto with a handful of men through the Kutsuki valley west of Lake Biwa. The deadliest post, the rearguard, was taken by Kinoshita Tōkichirō — Hideyoshi — with [[p:明智光秀|Akechi Mitsuhide]] and [[p:徳川家康|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], it is said.

Holding off the pursuing Asakura as they fell back, the rearguard saved Nobunaga, and made Hideyoshi's name.

title.en: The great return from the west

body.ja:
1582年六月二日、本能寺の変。そのとき[[p:羽柴秀吉]]は、備中の高松城を水攻めにして毛利軍と向き合っていた。翌日の夜、信長の死を知らせる明智方の密使が、秀吉の陣に迷い込んで捕らえられたという。

秀吉は信長の死を隠したまま、毛利と急いで和を結び、高松城主清水宗治の切腹を見届けると、全軍で東へ取って返した。およそ二百キロを十日足らずで駆け抜け、六月十三日、山崎で[[p:明智光秀]]を破った。

[[p:黒田官兵衛]]は、知らせを聞いて泣く秀吉に「ご運が開けましたな」とささやいたと伝わる。この速さが、秀吉を信長の後継ぎの座へと押し上げた。
body.en:
On the second day of the sixth month of 1582 came Honnōji. [[p:羽柴秀吉|Hashiba Hideyoshi]] was then flooding Takamatsu castle in Bitchū and facing the Mōri army. The next night, the story goes, a secret messenger of Akechi's wandered into Hideyoshi's lines and was caught.

Keeping Nobunaga's death secret, Hideyoshi hurriedly made peace with the Mōri, watched the castle's lord Shimizu Muneharu take his own life, and turned the whole army east — some two hundred kilometres in under ten days — to beat [[p:明智光秀|Akechi Mitsuhide]] at Yamazaki on the thirteenth.

[[p:黒田官兵衛|Kuroda Kanbei]], they say, whispered to the weeping Hideyoshi: "Your luck has opened." That speed carried Hideyoshi into Nobunaga's place.

body.ja:
1567年、美濃の[[p:斎藤龍興]]を追った[[p:織田信長]]は、稲葉山城と井ノ口の町に入り、町の名を「岐阜」と改めた。

名付けたのは、信長が招いた禅僧の沢彦宗恩だと伝わる。「岐」は、周の文王が岐山から起こって天下を取ったことに、「阜」は孔子の生まれた曲阜にちなむ。天下を取る志と、学問の地となる願いを込めた名だという (由来には諸説ある)。

この頃から信長は「天下布武」の印を使い始めた。岐阜は、信長が天下へ乗り出す足場となった。
body.en:
In 1567, having driven out [[p:斎藤龍興|Saitō Tatsuoki]] of Mino, [[p:織田信長|Oda Nobunaga]] took Inabayama castle and the town of Inokuchi below it, and renamed the town Gifu.

The name was chosen, they say, by the monk Takugen Sōon, whom Nobunaga had invited: "Gi" for Mount Qi, from which King Wen of Zhou rose to win the realm, and "fu" for Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius — ambition to rule the realm, and the hope of a seat of learning (accounts differ).

From about then Nobunaga began using his seal "Rule the realm by arms". Gifu was his springboard to the realm.

body.ja:
1570年、[[p:徳川家康]]は本拠を岡崎から遠江の引間城に移し、城を大きく築き直して「浜松城」と名を改めた。「引間」は「引く間」、つまり退くことに通じて縁起が悪い、と嫌ったためとも言われる。

家康は二十九歳から四十五歳までの十七年をこの城で過ごした。三方ヶ原で[[p:武田信玄]]に大敗して逃げ帰ったのもこの城である。

浜松城は、のちに城主となった者が幕府の要職に出世することが多かったため、「出世城」と呼ばれた。
body.en:
In 1570 [[p:徳川家康|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] moved his seat from Okazaki to Hikuma castle in Tōtōmi, rebuilt it on a large scale and renamed it Hamamatsu. "Hikuma" can be read as "time to draw back" — an ill omen for a warrior, they say.

Ieyasu spent seventeen years there, from twenty-nine to forty-five. It was to this castle that he fled after his great defeat by [[p:武田信玄|Takeda Shingen]] at Mikatagahara.

Since so many later lords of Hamamatsu rose to high office in the shogunate, it was nicknamed "the castle of promotion".

body.ja:
小田原征伐の後、[[p:伊達政宗]]から会津を取り上げた豊臣秀吉は、[[p:蒲生氏郷]]を会津の主とした。1592年、氏郷は黒川の町を「若松」と改め、七層の天守を持つ鶴ヶ城を築いた。

「若松」の名は、氏郷のふるさと近江日野の「若松の森」にちなむという。

氏郷は伊勢松坂から商人を呼び寄せ、楽市を開いて町を盛り立てた。会津は奥州をにらむ要の地であり、才ある氏郷が置かれたのは、政宗を抑えるためであった。
body.en:
After the Odawara campaign Toyotomi Hideyoshi took Aizu from [[p:伊達政宗|Date Masamune]] and gave it to [[p:蒲生氏郷|Gamō Ujisato]]. In 1592 Ujisato renamed the town of Kurokawa "Wakamatsu" and built Tsuruga castle with a seven-storey keep.

The name came, they say, from the "Wakamatsu wood" of Hino in Ōmi, Ujisato's home.

He brought merchants from [[p:まつ|Matsu]]saka in Ise, opened a free market and made the town thrive. Aizu watched over the north, and the able Ujisato was put there to hold Masamune in check.

body.ja:
1600年、[[p:伊達政宗]]は青葉山に新しい城を築き始め、城と町の名を「千代」から「仙台」に改めた。

唐の詩人の句に「仙臺 (仙人の住む高殿)」とあるのにちなむと伝わる。仙人の住むような長く栄える地となるよう、という願いを込めたという。

政宗は家臣の[[p:支倉常長]]をはるかスペインとローマへ使いに送るなど、天下人になれなかった野心を、海の向こうへ向けたとも言われる。
body.en:
In 1600 [[p:伊達政宗|Date Masamune]] began a new castle on Mount Aoba, and changed the name of the castle and town from "Sendai" written "a thousand ages" to "Sendai" written "terrace of the immortals".

The name is said to come from a line of a Tang poet mentioning a "terrace of the immortals" — a wish for a land that would flourish as long as the immortals live.

Masamune sent his retainer [[p:支倉常長|Hasekura Tsunenaga]] all the way to Spain and Rome — turning, some say, the ambition that could not win him the realm towards the lands beyond the sea.

body.ja:
肥後の[[p:加藤清正]]は、隈本城を大きく築き直し、1607年頃に完成させると、町の名を「隈本」から「熊本」に改めた。「隈」は「畏 (おそれる)」に通じて戦に向かないとして、勇ましい「熊」の字を用いたという。

熊本城は、高く反り返った石垣「武者返し」で知られる。朝鮮の陣で籠城の苦しさを知った清正は、城の中に井戸を百以上掘り、壁の中にかんぴょうや芋がらを塗り込めて、いざというときの食料にしたと伝わる。

二百七十年後の西南戦争で、熊本城は西郷隆盛の軍の攻撃に耐え抜いた。
body.en:
[[p:加藤清正|Katō Kiyomasa]] of Higo rebuilt Kumamoto castle on a grand scale, finishing around 1607, and changed the character of its name: the old "kuma" meant a nook, and sounded like "fear" — no name for war — so he used "kuma", bear.

The castle is famous for its steep, curving stone walls, the "warrior-repellers". Having learned the miseries of siege in Korea, Kiyomasa dug over a hundred wells inside and, they say, built dried gourd strips and taro stalks into the walls as food for a last stand.

Two hundred and seventy years later, in the Satsuma rebellion, Kumamoto castle held out against the army of Saigō Takamori.

ties.ja: 草履取りから仕えた秀吉を、信長は「猿」「禿げ鼠」と呼んで可愛がり、重く用いた。
ties.en: Nobunaga called Hideyoshi, who began as his sandal-bearer, "monkey" and "bald rat", and raised him high.

ties.ja: 信長の弟信勝に従って背いた勝家は、許されてからは織田家の筆頭の将となった。
ties.en: Katsuie once rebelled with Nobunaga's brother; pardoned, he became the first of Oda's generals.

ties.ja: 1582年、光秀は本能寺の信長を襲った。理由は今も謎である。
ties.en: In 1582 Mitsuhide fell on Nobunaga at Honnōji — why is still a mystery.

ties.ja: 利家は若い頃「槍の又左」と呼ばれた信長の側近であった。
ties.en: In his youth Toshiie was one of Nobunaga's pages, "Mataza of the spear".

ties.ja: 牛一は信長の一代記『信長公記』を書き残した。
ties.en: [[p:太田牛一|Ōta Gyūichi]] wrote Nobunaga's chronicle.

ties.ja: 永徳は安土城の障壁画を描いた。
ties.en: Eitoku painted the walls of Azuchi castle.

ties.ja: 信長はフロイスと十数回も会い、遠い国々の話を好んで聞いた。
ties.en: Nobunaga met Frois more than a dozen times, eager to hear of faraway lands.

ties.ja: 信長の妹[[p:お市]]を妻に迎えながら、長政は朝倉との古い盟約を選び、金ヶ崎で信長を挟み撃ちにしかけた。
ties.en: Married to Nobunaga's sister [[p:お市|Oichi]], Nagamasa chose his old alliance with the Asakura and nearly trapped Nobunaga at Kanegasaki.

ties.ja: 久秀は二度にわたって信長に背き、最後は信貴山城で滅んだ。
ties.en: Hisahide rebelled against Nobunaga twice, and perished at last at Shigisan.

ties.ja: 有岡城で信長に背いた村重は、説得に来た[[p:黒田官兵衛]]を一年も土牢に閉じ込めた。
ties.en: Rebelling at Arioka, Murashige threw [[p:黒田官兵衛|Kuroda Kanbei]], who came to talk him round, into a dungeon for a year.

ties.ja: 官兵衛が裏切ったと思い込んだ信長に、官兵衛の子を殺せと命じられた半兵衛は、ひそかに子をかくまって救った。
ties.en: Ordered by Nobunaga, who thought Kanbei a traitor, to kill Kanbei's son, Hanbei hid the boy and saved him.

ties.ja: 秀吉は官兵衛の才を恐れ、「わしの後に天下を取るのはあの男だ」と言ったという。
ties.en: Hideyoshi feared Kanbei's gifts: "the one who will take the realm after me is that man," he is said to have remarked.

ties.ja: 「三献の茶」。寺の小僧だった三成は、喉の渇いた秀吉にぬるい茶をたっぷり、次に少し熱く、最後に熱い茶を少しだけ出し、その気配りで召し抱えられたという。
ties.en: "Three cups of tea." As a temple boy, Mitsunari served the thirsty Hideyoshi a big cup of lukewarm tea, then a smaller, hotter one, then a little very hot — and was taken into his service for his thoughtfulness, the story goes.

ties.ja: 賤ヶ岳で手柄を立てた「七本槍」の一人。
ties.en: One of the "Seven Spears" of Shizugatake.

ties.ja: 七本槍の筆頭。
ties.en: First of the Seven Spears.

ties.ja: 茶頭として重んじた利休に、秀吉は1591年、切腹を命じた。
ties.en: In 1591 Hideyoshi ordered Rikyū, his honoured tea master, to take his own life.

ties.ja: 弟の秀長は秀吉を陰で支え、秀長が死ぬと豊臣家に影がさした。
ties.en: His brother Hidenaga was his steady support; when Hidenaga died a shadow fell over the house.

ties.ja: 茶会で、病の吉継の膿が茶碗に落ち、皆が飲むのをためらった。三成は平然と飲み干したという。吉継は負けると知りながら三成のために関ヶ原で戦った。
ties.en: At a tea gathering pus from the sick Yoshitsugu's face fell into the shared bowl and no one would drink; Mitsunari drank it off, the story goes. Yoshitsugu fought for him at Sekigahara knowing they would lose.

ties.ja: 朝鮮の陣以来、武断派の清正・正則らと三成は激しく対立した。
ties.en: From the Korean campaigns the fighting generals Kiyomasa and Masanori loathed Mitsunari.

ties.ja: 関ヶ原の昼過ぎ、松尾山の秀秋は東軍に寝返った。
ties.en: Past noon at Sekigahara, Hideaki on Mount [[p:まつ|Matsu]]o went over to the east.

ties.ja: 五十余度の戦で傷一つ負わなかったという猛将。「家康に過ぎたるもの」とうたわれた。
ties.en: A fierce warrior said never to have been wounded in fifty-odd battles — "more than Ieyasu deserves", people sang.

ties.ja: 本能寺の変の後、半蔵は家康を伊賀の山越えで三河へ逃がした。
ties.en: After Honnōji Hanzō led Ieyasu to safety over the hills of Iga.

ties.ja: 家康は正信を「友」と呼び、二人きりで長く語り合ったという。
ties.en: Ieyasu called Masanobu his "friend", and talked with him alone for hours.

ties.ja: 1585年、家康の重臣数正は突然秀吉のもとへ走った。
ties.en: In 1585 Kazumasa, one of Ieyasu's chief retainers, suddenly went over to Hideyoshi.

ties.ja: 五度の川中島。信玄が死んだと聞いた謙信は、食事の箸を落として泣いたという。
ties.en: Five battles at Kawanakajima. Hearing Shingen was dead, Kenshin dropped his chopsticks and wept, they say.

ties.ja: 無口な景勝と才気の兼続は、生涯の主従であった。
ties.en: Silent Kagekatsu and brilliant Kanetsugu were lord and retainer for life.

ties.ja: 幼い政宗の、病で飛び出した右目を、景綱が小刀で切り取ったという話が伝わる。
ties.en: The story goes that Kagetsuna cut out with a knife the young Masamune's eye, which disease had made bulge.

ties.ja: 大友家の二つの柱。道雪は紹運の子宗茂を婿養子に迎えた。
ties.en: The two pillars of the Ōtomo; Dōsetsu adopted Jōun's son Muneshige as his heir.

ties.ja: 「願わくば我に七難八苦を与えたまえ」。尼子家の再興に生涯をかけた。
ties.en: "Grant me seven troubles and eight sorrows." He gave his life to restoring the Amago.

ties.ja: 天下一の絵師の座を争った二人。
ties.en: Rivals for the title of first painter of the realm.

ties.ja: 1612年、巌流島で二人は決闘し、遅れて来た武蔵が櫂を削った木刀で小次郎を倒したと伝わる。
ties.en: In 1612 they duelled on Ganryūjima; Musashi, arriving late, struck Kojirō down with a sword carved from an oar, so the story goes.

ties.ja: 大坂の陣で豊臣方の牢人衆を率いた二人。又兵衛は道明寺で討死した。
ties.en: The two led the masterless warriors on the Toyotomi side at Osaka; Matabei died at Dōmyōji.

ties.ja: 氏郷は右近に導かれてキリスト教に親しんだ。
ties.en: Ujisato came to Christianity through Ukon.

ties.ja: 人質だった少年氏郷の才を見抜いた信長は、娘を嫁がせた。
ties.en: Seeing the gifts of the boy hostage, Nobunaga gave him his daughter in marriage.

ties.ja: 光秀の娘玉 (ガラシャ) は藤孝の子忠興の妻。だが本能寺の後、藤孝は髪を下ろして光秀に味方しなかった。
ties.en: Mitsuhide's daughter Tama (Gracia) was married to Fujitaka's son; yet after Honnōji Fujitaka shaved his head and would not join Mitsuhide.

marriages.ja: 美濃の斎藤道三の娘帰蝶 ([[p:濃姫]])。尾張と美濃の和を結ぶ政略の結婚であった。道三は娘に短刀を持たせ、「信長がうつけなら刺せ」と言うと、娘は「この刀は父上を刺すことになるかもしれません」と答えた、という話が伝わる。
marriages.en: Kichō ([[p:濃姫|Lady Nō]]), daughter of Saitō Dōsan of Mino: a political match sealing peace between Owari and Mino. Dōsan, the story goes, gave her a dagger to kill Nobunaga if he proved a fool; she answered that it might be her father she used it on.

marriages.ja: 身分の違いを越えた、当時には珍しい恋愛による結婚とも言われる。[[p:ねね]]はのちに北政所と呼ばれ、秀吉の天下を内から支えた。信長はねねに、秀吉の浮気を戒める手紙を送り「あの禿げ鼠にはそなた以上の妻は見つからぬ」と書いている。
marriages.en: A love match across ranks, rare in that age, it is said. [[p:ねね|Nene]], later called Kita-no-Mandokoro, upheld Hideyoshi's rule from within. Nobunaga wrote her a letter about Hideyoshi's philandering: "that bald rat will never find a better wife than you."

marriages.ja: 信長の妹[[p:お市]]は、北近江の[[p:浅井長政]]に嫁いだ。織田と浅井の同盟の証であった。長政が信長に背き、小谷城が落ちたとき、お市は三人の娘 (茶々・初・江) とともに織田の陣へ送り返された。
marriages.en: Nobunaga's sister [[p:お市|Oichi]] married [[p:浅井長政|Azai Nagamasa]] of northern Ōmi, the pledge of the Oda–Azai alliance. When Nagamasa turned on Nobunaga and Odani fell, Oichi and her three daughters — Chacha, Hatsu and Gō — were sent back to the Oda camp.

marriages.ja: 本能寺の後、清洲会議を経て[[p:お市]]は[[p:柴田勝家]]に再嫁した。翌年、賤ヶ岳で勝家が秀吉に敗れると、二人は北ノ庄城で共に自害した。娘たちは城から逃された。
marriages.en: After Honnōji and the Kiyosu council, [[p:お市|Oichi]] remarried [[p:柴田勝家|Shibata Katsuie]]. The next year Katsuie was beaten by Hideyoshi at Shizugatake, and the two killed themselves together at Kitanoshō; the daughters were sent out of the castle.

marriages.ja: [[p:お市]]の長女茶々は、かつて母を死に追いやった秀吉の側室となった。淀城を与えられて[[p:淀殿]]と呼ばれ、秀頼を生んだ。
marriages.en: [[p:お市|Oichi]]'s eldest daughter Chacha became the concubine of Hideyoshi, the man who had driven her mother to her death. Given Yodo castle, she was called [[p:淀殿|Lady Yodo]], and bore Hideyori.

marriages.ja: [[p:今川義元]]の姪を母に持つ[[p:築山殿]]は、今川家の人質だった若い家康の妻となった。1579年、武田に通じたと疑われ、子の信康とともに死を命じられた。
marriages.en: [[p:築山殿|Lady Tsukiyama]], whose mother was a niece of [[p:今川義元|Imagawa Yoshimoto]], married the young Ieyasu while he was an Imagawa hostage. In 1579, suspected of dealings with the Takeda, she was put to death, and her son Nobuyasu ordered to kill himself.

marriages.ja: [[p:まつ]]は十二歳で利家に嫁いだ。のちに利家が秀吉と[[p:柴田勝家]]の間で迷ったとき、秀吉との間を取り持ったのはまつであった。関ヶ原の前には自ら江戸へ人質に下り、前田家を守った。
marriages.en: [[p:まつ|Matsu]] married Toshiie at twelve. When Toshiie wavered between Hideyoshi and [[p:柴田勝家|Shibata Katsuie]], it was she who made his peace with Hideyoshi; before Sekigahara she went to Edo herself as a hostage to keep the Maeda safe.

marriages.ja: [[p:お市]]の三女江は、三度目の結婚で家康の子秀忠に嫁ぎ、三代将軍家光を生んだ。姉の[[p:淀殿]]は大坂城で徳川と戦い、妹の江は徳川の妻として生きた。
marriages.en: [[p:お市|Oichi]]'s third daughter Gō, on her third marriage, wed Ieyasu's son Hidetada and bore the third shogun, Iemitsu. Her elder sister [[p:淀殿|Lady Yodo]] fought the Tokugawa at Osaka; Gō lived as a Tokugawa wife.

marriages.ja: 家康の孫[[p:千姫]]は、七歳で秀頼に嫁いだ。秀吉との約束を果たす政略の結婚であった。大坂夏の陣で、千姫は燃える城から救い出された。
marriages.en: Ieyasu's granddaughter Sen married Hideyori at seven, keeping a promise made to Hideyoshi. In the summer siege of Osaka she was rescued from the burning castle.

marriages.ja: 田村家の娘[[p:愛姫]]は、十二歳で政宗に嫁いだ。田村家との同盟が伊達の南奥州での足場となった。
marriages.en: Megohime of the Tamura married Masamune at twelve; the Tamura alliance was the Date foothold in southern Ōu.
